h.strategy: Naive reasoning predicts substitution: if something similar exists elsewhere, an edit helps less. Experts find this obvious, so at most two hypotheses may use it. At least three hypotheses must predict the opposite, complementarity, where an edit helps MORE because a different kind of component elsewhere supplies what it lacks. At least two must predict a reversal, where a usually beneficial edit becomes harmful under a specific condition through trainability, merged-signal scale, or over-capacity. Never condition on the edited field's own value or on settings that make the edit inert. Each hypothesis must couple two different fields, and no condition setting may appear more than twice. In each 'why', give the mechanism in two or three sentences, state why an expert might bet the other way, and name the refuting comparison. The critic should replace any hypothesis that duplicates another's mechanism.

hyps.why: A skip on 0->3 already gives node 3 a strong baseline path, so adding conv3x3 on edge 4 gains less.
Setting edge 3 to none changes nothing when it is already none, whereas it removes a useful path otherwise.
With edge 4 absent, removing edge 3 leaves node 3 dependent on the single path through edge 5.
With a conv3x3 already feeding node 3 via edge 4, a second conv3x3 on edge 5 shows diminishing returns.
A skip on edge 3 already secures node 3, so extra conv capacity on edge 5 adds less.
Without the direct 0->3 edge, input must reach node 3 via nodes 1 and 2, so removing edge 1 cuts a critical route.
When edge 3 is absent, edge 4 is a main route to the output, so removing it costs more.
When edge 5 is absent node 3 is poorly connected, so a skip on 0->3 gives a larger gain.
Adding conv3x3 on edge 3 gains most when it replaces none rather than an already useful op.
A conv3x3 on edge 5 provides a strong alternative input to node 3, so dropping the direct edge hurts less.
